summary: Dividing a fraction by a fraction is where invert-and-multiply ('keep-change-flip') completes: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6. The risk is that it becomes a meaningless ritual — students fail to invert either fraction (→ 8/15), invert the wrong fraction, or invert both. The teaching goal is to bind the rule to meaning: read it as a measurement ('how many 4/5s fit into 2/3?' — a bit less than one), model that, contrast correct and misapplied methods, derive why only the divisor inverts, and use estimation to guard the answer.
misconceptions: Does not invert either fraction — just multiplies: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 8/15 (IES)
Inverts the wrong fraction — flips the dividend: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 3/2 × 4/5 (IES)
Applies keep-change-flip correctly but as a rote rule — cannot model it, justify the flip, or judge if the answer is reasonable

activities.title: Measure it and run the rule side by side
steps: Take a bar representing 2/3 and lay 4/5-length bars into it; find that not even one whole 4/5 fits, and read how much of a 4/5 does fit (about 5/6 of one).
Alongside, run keep-change-flip: keep 2/3, change ÷ to ×, flip ONLY the 4/5 to 5/4, and compute 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6.
Confirm the measured amount (5/6 of a 4/5 fits) and the rule's answer (5/6) agree.
Deliberately flip the wrong fraction (3/2 × 4/5 = 6/5) or both (3/2 × 5/4 = 15/8) and compare each result to the measured 5/6 — notice how far each wrong flip lands from what you measured.
activities.insight: Inverting the divisor is not an arbitrary trick: the rule's answer matches the measured 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3', and flipping the dividend or both pulls the answer away from that measured amount.

activities.title: Derive why only the divisor inverts
steps: Start from 2/3 ÷ 4/5 and multiply both the dividend and the divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor, 5/4: (2/3 × 5/4) ÷ (4/5 × 5/4).
State in your own words why the dividend 2/3 is left untouched and only the divisor is turned into 1.
Explain, using this derivation, why flipping both fractions (3/2 × 5/4) is wrong — the dividend was never inverted.
activities.insight: Invert-and-multiply can be derived rather than asserted: multiplying dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor makes the divisor 1, leaving dividend × reciprocal, which is why only the divisor flips.

activities.title: Estimate before you compute
steps: Before calculating 2/3 ÷ 4/5, note that 4/5 is close to 1, so 2/3 ÷ 4/5 should be close to 2/3 ÷ 1 = 2/3, and a bit more than 2/3 because you are dividing by a little less than 1.
After computing, check whether your answer (5/6) is more than 2/3 (2/3 = 10/15, 5/6 ≈ 12.5/15) — it is.
Use the estimate to reject answers like 6/5 (too big) or 8/15 (less than 2/3, wrong direction).
activities.insight: A quick estimate of the expected size catches inverted-wrong-fraction and no-flip blunders before they are accepted.

activities.title: Diagnose the method, not just the answer
steps: Work out 2/3 ÷ 4/5 showing every step of the method.
Then draw a picture or tell a story that shows what 2/3 ÷ 4/5 actually means.
Transfer the method to a new case, e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4, and say whether the answer is bigger or smaller than 1/2 and why.
Match each wrong result — 8/15, 6/5, 15/8 — to the mistake that produced it (no flip, wrong fraction flipped, both flipped).
activities.insight: Owning fraction division means producing the answer, modelling or story-ing the division, justifying why only the divisor flips, and judging the answer's reasonableness — not just reciting the steps.

activities.title: Defend each step to a questioner
steps: Present each step of 2/3 ÷ 4/5 to a partner or tutor who keeps asking 'why?' and refuses 'because that's the rule' as an answer.
Justify why the division becomes a multiplication, why only the second fraction flips, and why 5/6 is reasonable.
Answer the follow-up: how would the answer change if you flipped the other fraction instead?
activities.insight: Being pressed for justification can expose a merely rote rule and can push the learner to connect the procedure to the reciprocal derivation and the measurement meaning.

checkQuestion: Work out 2/3 ÷ 4/5, showing every step of your method. Then draw a picture or tell a story that shows what 2/3 ÷ 4/5 actually means.
checkAnswer: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6. Meaning: 'how many 4/5s fit into 2/3?' — a bit less than one whole 4/5 fits, namely 5/6 of it. (Or common denominators: 10/15 ÷ 12/15 = 10/12 = 5/6.)
